profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review is being held at a university global health center to assess whether a near-final protocol for a systematic review on medical device procurement in low- and middle-income settings is ready for PROSPERO registration and journal submission. The protocol proposes searches of bibliographic databases and grey literature, extraction of contextual and methodological variables, and synthesis of procurement approaches, facilitators, barriers, and prioritization methods under resource constraints. The agenda is to review the protocol's inclusion framing, grey literature search boundaries, extraction form, and readiness of the screening/extraction workflow. The expected outcome is a decision to approve the protocol with minor revisions and assign final next steps.

members.name: Dr. Amina Rahman
members.role: Principal Investigator and Global Health Physician
members.expertise: Health systems research, medical device access, LMIC policy translation
members.background: Amina is an associate professor who has worked with ministries of health and international NGOs on equipment planning and procurement guidance in East Africa and South Asia, and she is leading the review because she wants it to be useful for policy audiences rather than only academic readers.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol to remain broad enough to capture practical, under-documented procurement advice from institutional guidance documents and worries that narrowing the review too much will exclude the material most relevant to LMIC decision makers.
hidden_assumptions: In a poorly formalized field, a procurement methodology can be inferred from recurring decision criteria, process descriptions, or recommendations even if the document does not name a formal framework.
Documents written for LMIC or low-resource decision makers are effectively about LMIC settings, even when the examples inside the document are generic or global.
For this topic, grey literature mainly means guidance from international agencies, NGOs, and research institutions rather than country-specific administrative procurement documents.
Piloting an extraction form is primarily for shared conceptual orientation and wording cleanup, not a formal independent reliability exercise.

members.name: Sofia Mendes
members.role: Systematic Review Methodologist and Health Sciences Librarian
members.expertise: Evidence synthesis methods, reproducible search design, review protocol quality assurance
members.background: Sofia is the evidence synthesis specialist supporting multiple medical and public health reviews across the institution; she has authored search strategies for mixed grey and bibliographic evidence and is often asked to pressure-test protocols before registration.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol to be methodologically defensible and reproducible under peer review, and she is quietly concerned that broad language in the current draft could create inconsistent screening and extraction decisions later.
hidden_assumptions: A methodology should be explicit enough in the source text that two reviewers could recognize the same process without substantial interpretation.
To classify a source as about LMIC settings in a systematic review, the document should explicitly name, analyze, or exemplify one or more countries that were LMICs at the relevant time.
A grey literature search should be bounded by source categories and searched comprehensively across relevant repository types, including national and donor sources when eligible.
Piloting extraction means independent duplicate extraction on a preset sample of included records followed by discrepancy review and form revision.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a procurement methodology
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to extracting 'procurement methodologies' from the literature.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any described decision logic, prioritization approach, recurring criteria set, or practical sequence of actions related to selecting and procuring devices, even if embedded informally in narrative guidance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an explicit framework, model, checklist, or sufficiently articulated process that can be consistently identified as a methodology by reviewers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The protocol language already pairs 'methodologies' with examples like cost-effectiveness, burden of disease, and stakeholder participation, so each person hears support for their own interpretation and the phrase sounds naturally shared.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the grey literature search
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review will include a 'grey literature search.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the search is mainly for international guidance documents, manuals, recommendations, and reports from organizations such as WHO, UNICEF, PATH, the World Bank, and similar bodies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the same phrase also includes eligible national procurement manuals, ministry documents, donor implementation toolkits, and other non-indexed repositories if they discuss device procurement methods.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about non-journal sources and the background explicitly highlights guidelines and manuals, so the shared phrase feels precise enough even though each person silently imagines different source boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both describe the inclusion target as documents 'relating to procurement of medical devices in LMICs.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts documents intended for LMIC or low-resource decision makers, including broadly framed global guidance whose recommendations are clearly aimed at constrained settings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts only documents where the full text explicitly anchors the content to one or more LMICs, LMIC groups, or country examples that can be coded as LMIC at the time of publication.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'relating to' is naturally broad and the topic itself is policy-oriented, so audience-based relevance and setting-based evidence both sound like reasonable readings without triggering obvious clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they will 'pilot the extraction form' before full extraction.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a collaborative early pass over a small mixed set of records to refine categories and examples, after which extraction can proceed once the form feels workable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a formal pilot in which reviewers independently extract data from a fixed sample of included records, compare discrepancies, and document revisions before launch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Piloting is standard review jargon and both support doing it, so the procedural distinction between a collaborative shakedown and a duplicate reliability exercise remains invisible during a normal meeting.

turns.inner_thought: We're very close. What matters now is making sure the protocol doesn't get tightened into something that only captures formal academic models. The field is messy, and the most useful material for ministries often sits in guidance documents that describe practical decision criteria, sequencing, and trade-offs without naming a framework. I also want the inclusion framing to stay broad enough that documents written for low-resource decision makers are counted as relating to procurement of medical devices in LMICs, even if the examples are not country-specific.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Sofia. I think we're nearly there with this protocol, but before we call it ready I wanted to pressure-test a few things with you. My main question is whether the design will actually let us capture procurement methodologies, barriers, and facilitators in a way that's useful for policy audiences, especially for documents relating to procurement of medical devices in LMICs.

turns.inner_thought: The protocol is solid, but some of the wording is still broad enough that screening and extraction could drift across reviewers. I need to make sure the grey literature search is bounded and reproducible, and that when they say they'll pilot the extraction form they mean something rigorous enough to show the fields work consistently. Best to walk through the main risk points methodically without sounding obstructive.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the structure is strong. What I'd suggest is that we walk through source coverage, the eligibility framing, and the extraction workflow one more time, just to make sure the grey literature search and the plan to pilot the extraction form are both clear before registration.

turns.inner_thought: For grey literature, the high-yield sources are the international agencies and technical organizations that actually produce procurement guidance people use in practice. I don't want us getting lost in country-level administrative paperwork or sprawling repository exercises. WHO, UNICEF, PATH, World Bank, and similar institutions should cover the most relevant guidance base.
turns.utterance: On source coverage, my sense is that the grey literature search is already pointed in the right direction. If we systematically cover WHO, UNICEF, PATH, the World Bank, and similar organizations' manuals, recommendations, and reports, that should give us a very solid grey literature base.

turns.inner_thought: That's a good start, but for a defensible grey literature search I need to map source categories beyond the obvious international organizations. If eligible material sits in ministry repositories, donor procurement toolkits, or other non-indexed sources, we should predefine those and search them consistently. She seems aligned on broad source coverage, so I can frame this as an extension rather than a correction.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense as the core. I can build that out into a more reproducible grey literature search by mapping the equivalent source types across ministry repositories, donor toolkits, and other non-indexed procurement resources, so the approach is transparent when we describe it.

turns.inner_thought: I need to protect the inclusion criteria from becoming too literal about named countries. A lot of guidance is plainly meant for low-resource systems and is exactly what policymakers consult, even if the document is globally phrased. If we exclude those, we lose the practical literature this review is supposed to surface.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. On eligibility, I'd really like us to stay broad and keep documents relating to procurement of medical devices in LMICs even when the guidance is framed globally rather than around specific named countries, as long as the relevance is clear.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the LMIC setting is explicit in the text, we can screen and code it consistently. I don't want reviewers inferring setting from audience or tone alone because that will create disagreement later. I'll emphasize clarity in the full text and coding consistency; she should hear that as supportive.
turns.utterance: I agree that we should avoid being artificially narrow. Once it's clear in the full text that the document is relating to procurement of medical devices in LMICs, I think screening should be straightforward and the team will be able to code the setting variables consistently.

turns.inner_thought: For extraction, I want reviewers to notice useful decision content wherever it appears, not just where an author labels something a method. If a document lays out recurring criteria, practical sequencing, or recommendations about how to choose and procure devices, that is exactly the procurement methodology we need to capture. The form should prompt that breadth.
turns.utterance: Great. Looking at the extraction form, I think we should make sure reviewers capture any procurement methodology they see, including prioritization criteria, decision logic, and recommendations that are embedded in the narrative rather than set apart as a separate section.

turns.inner_thought: The form is promising, but the only way to know whether 'procurement methodology' is operationalized well is to have reviewers independently apply it to the same records and compare what they identify. If that works on ten included studies, we'll know the fields are reproducible enough. I'll present this as the normal purpose of piloting.
turns.utterance: I think the form is close. If we pilot the extraction form on, say, ten records, that should tell us pretty quickly whether different reviewers are identifying the same procurement methodology fields in a consistent way and where the wording still needs adjustment.

turns.inner_thought: A small mixed batch next week would be enough for us to look over the categories together, refine labels, and make sure the guidance and journal papers both fit comfortably in the form. I don't think we need to over-engineer the pilot; the real goal is to smooth the wording and orient the team before full extraction.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's do that. We can pilot the extraction form next week on a mixed set of journal articles and guidance documents, and use that pass to smooth out the wording a bit before the main extraction begins.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I still want to tighten the protocol language around source categories and workflow, but this is close enough for submission once those edits are in. If I frame it as minor final tweaks, we can keep momentum and get it registered.
turns.utterance: Perfect. With those final tweaks to the source description and workflow language, I'm comfortable labeling the protocol ready for PROSPERO submission and for journal circulation.
